rv.q: If the entire dream cast of Terrence McNally's backstage revenge play had less than split-millisecond timing, the merciless inside-showbiz observations about the theater and theaterfolk might wound deeper than they amuse.
Lane has the best comic timing in the business, and it really is a joy to watch him as he savors every drop of McNally's venomous humor.

Whatever it is, it's a pure hoot, a rollicking comedy with perfect casting and deft direction in Jack O'Brien that gleefully dissects modern Broadway and doesn't pretend to mask its targets by using fake names.
McNeal's play is a lightweight but genuinely funny backstage comedy that provides a perfect vehicle for this stellar cast to showcase their considerable comic talents.
Lane indeed carries the show on his capable shoulders, doling out the cutting lines and abashed double-takes as expertly as a Las Vegas croupier at a gaming table.
He might as well be talking about the comedy in which he appears, which is directed with gusto by Jack O’Brien.
McNally's farcical doodle starts out like gangbusters but becomes increasingly uneven.

Without a credible force representing the active hopes for a meaningful theater, It’s Only a Play skews way to the downside and, hilarious though it often is, comes off as too much of a personal pity party.
As directed by Jack O'Brien, it is also a depressingly uneven production.
Those who revel in Broadway mythology, though, will forgive the shortcomings (and drawn-out speechifying) of 'It's Only a Play' and enjoy some of the better skewering of theater archetypes.
Mullally and Lane alone are almost worth the price of admission, with a sense of timing that’s a thing of wonder.
Mostly plotless and spun from the sketchiest of stereotypes and hoariest of showbiz prejudices, this insider trifle is too long, too shallow and not nearly funny enough.
Lane whips the audience into fits of laughter, both jaded and joyful, from the moment James enters, promptly dialing his Hollywood agent to wax snarky about his buddy's show.
The play itself... remains as sharp and funny as ever, skewering the theatrical world with surgical precision.
It's Only a Play is a poison-pen mash note to New York theater, at once gleefully bitchy and affectionate.
Many of the jokes would fail if not for Lane, Broderick and their savvy director, Jack O’Brien.

Theatergoers will get their money's worth, if you can calculate worth by belly laffs, but it turns out that McNally's It's Only a Play is not all that much better than the play-within-a-play that the characters spend the night lamenting.
Theater insiders, on the other hand, will guffaw at the inside cracks about online Broadway chat rooms, but many will feel “It’s Only a Play” lazily misses its mark.
While act one offers plenty of silly, lightweight fun, the play essentially collapses in the self-indulgent, overly sentimental act two.
Despite astute and acclaimed work in plays like “Master Class” and musicals including “Ragtime,” McNally’s writing here is uneven.
But holy David Merrick — what a mess.
Yet despite the tired quips, director Jack O’Brien and the brilliant Lane keep the audience howling.

tn.cat: Best Featured Actor in a Play

cn.t: McNally's insider Broadway satire delivers sharp zingers and laughs, elevated by Lane's comic brilliance, though critics find the material lightweight and dated beneath the star power.
